q: You engage astern from rest. Which way does the stern kick?
a: To port
o: To starboard
Neither — she backs straight
Towards the nearer pontoon
why: A right-handed propeller walks the stern to port when going astern.

q: You must turn the boat round in this fairway. Which way do you turn?
a: To starboard — prop walk astern helps
o: To port — prop walk astern helps
Either way — prop walk has no effect
To port — the rudder works best that way
why: Astern, a right-handed prop kicks the stern to port, which swings the bow to starboard.

q: Leaving the pontoon, you steer to starboard to move away. What does your stern do?
a: Swings to port, towards the pontoon
o: Swings to starboard, away from it
Stays put; only the bow moves
Follows the bow out to starboard
why: Going ahead a boat pivots well forward, so the stern swings the opposite way to the bow.

fig.title: Leaving along the pontoon
lines: Pontoon close on your port side

q: You are drifting almost stopped, engine in neutral, and turn the wheel hard over. Why does the boat not turn?
a: No water is flowing past the rudder
o: The rudder only works in reverse
The wheel must turn twice as far
The keel stops her turning at rest
why: A rudder steers only when water flows over it — from boat speed or prop wash.

q: You are stopped in a marina and want the bow to swing to starboard without gathering speed. What do you do?
a: Wheel to starboard, short burst ahead
o: Wheel to starboard, steady slow astern
Wheel amidships, long burst ahead
Wheel to port, short burst ahead
why: Prop wash over the turned rudder swings the boat before she picks up way.

q: You are reversing down the fairway when the wheel suddenly spins out of your hand and the boat swerves. What should you have done?
a: Held the wheel firmly and gone slower
o: Let the wheel centre itself
Gone astern faster to steer better
Locked the wheel with the autopilot
why: Going astern the rudder tries to slam over; hold the wheel firmly and keep the speed low.

q: You slow right down in this fairway. What does the bow do?
a: Blows off downwind, to port
o: Turns up into the wind, to starboard
Holds straight — the keel stops it
Stays put while the stern blows off
why: At low speed the high bow catches more wind than the keel can resist, so it blows off downwind.

q: You are about to come alongside the fuel berth. How fast do you approach?
a: No faster than you'd want to hit it
o: Fast, then full astern at the last moment
At cruising speed, to keep steering
Any speed — the fenders take the knock
why: Approach at a speed you could accept hitting at — slow, with just enough way to steer.

q: You use the bow thruster to push the bow off the pontoon. How do you use it?
a: In short bursts, with pauses between
o: Held on until you are well clear
Only at cruising speed, to help a turn
Switched rapidly left and right
why: Bow thrusters overheat and cut out if run for long; use short bursts.

q: You reverse out of this berth. How do you start?
a: Gently astern, letting the rudder take over
o: A hard burst astern to get out quickly
Wheel hard over first, then full astern
Ahead first, to swing the stern to port
why: Prop walk is strongest from rest at high revs; go gently so way builds and the rudder steers.

fig.title: Bow-in finger berth
lines: Neighbour close on your port side

q: You can lie either side of this pontoon and will stop with a touch of astern. Which side do you choose?
a: Port side to — astern pulls the stern in
o: Starboard side to — astern pulls the stern in
Port side to — astern pushes the stern out
Either — prop walk only acts from rest
why: Going astern to stop, a right-handed prop walks the stern to port — onto a port-side berth.

q: A boat is leaving a berth ahead and you must wait in this fairway. How do you hold position?
a: Head to wind, with short bursts ahead
o: In neutral, letting her drift
Beam-on to the wind, in neutral
Circling the fairway at cruising speed
why: Head to wind the bow cannot blow off, and short bursts ahead hold you in place.

fig.title: Waiting to enter
lines: Wind F4 straight down the fairway

q: You are coming alongside here. How do you approach?
a: At a steeper angle, getting a line on fast
o: Parallel, stopping off to drift in
Stern first, with plenty of speed
Very slowly, in neutral from far out
why: When the wind blows you off, come in at a steeper angle and get the bow line on quickly.

fig.title: Coming alongside
lines: Wind F4 blowing off the pontoon

q: You are reversing slowly down this fairway with the wind on your port beam. What do you expect?
a: The stern swings to port, into the wind
o: The stern swings to starboard, downwind
She backs straight; the two cancel out
The bow swings to port, into the wind
why: The bow blows off downwind and prop walk kicks the stern to port: both swing the stern to port.

q: You are motoring slowly ahead and need to go astern. How do you shift?
a: Pause in neutral, then engage astern
o: Straight from ahead into astern
Stop the engine, then restart astern
Rev up in neutral, then go astern
why: A pause in neutral lets the propeller slow down and saves the gearbox.

q: You are turning to starboard in your own length. After the short burst ahead, what comes next?
a: Neutral, short burst astern, wheel unchanged
o: A long burst astern to build sternway
Wheel to port, then full ahead
Engine off — let the wind finish it
why: Short bursts ahead and astern turn her in her own length; prop walk astern adds to the turn.

q: Coming into your berth, a gust pushes you off line towards a neighbour's bow. What do you do?
a: Abort, motor clear and try again
o: Push on faster to force your way in
Fend off with a foot between boats
Stop there and wait for the gust to pass
why: If an approach goes wrong, go round again — never fend off with hands or feet.

q: Going astern at 2 knots, you want the stern to move to starboard. Which way do you turn the wheel?
a: To starboard — the stern follows the wheel
o: To port — the stern goes against the wheel
Amidships, and wait for prop walk
Either way — it makes no difference astern
why: With a wheel, going astern the stern moves the way you turn the wheel.

q: Your crew want to motor in fast "so the wind can't push us about". What is your call?
a: Just enough speed to steer, no more
o: Fast, to be through before it acts
Dead slow in neutral, drifting through
Cruising speed, thruster on all the way
why: Too slow and the wind takes the bow; too fast and you cannot stop — keep just steerage way.

fig.title: Entering the marina
lines: Narrow fairways, boats on both sides

q: You reverse out of this berth and turn down the fairway. What do you watch most closely?
a: Your bow swinging to starboard
o: Your stern swinging to starboard
Your bow swinging to port
Nothing — she backs out straight
why: Going astern the pivot point moves aft, so the bow swings wide the opposite way to the stern.

fig.title: Reversing out
lines: Neighbours' bows close on both sides
You steer the stern to port
